opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, for a long time I just didn't see myself as that kind of person. My identity was built around mathematics. Since I was a teenager, the thing that excited me most was sitting with a hard problem for days, sometimes weeks, and finally seeing the structure underneath it. That's a very quiet, very internal kind of joy. When I pictured an entrepreneur, I pictured someone who loves pitching, networking, managing people, closing deals. I didn't think that was me.

There was also the path I was already on. I was in a PhD program, I had advisors I respected, and there was a very clear trajectory: do good research, write papers, maybe become a professor someday. That path felt safe and meaningful. Leaving it felt like admitting I didn't want to be a "real" mathematician anymore, and I struggled with that for a while.

And frankly, I was a bit afraid. In research, if you fail, it's mostly your own time you've lost. As a founder, you're asking people to quit their jobs and join you, asking investors to trust you with their money. That responsibility felt heavy, and I wasn't sure I was ready to carry it.

What changed my mind was realizing the question I cared about, whether AI can truly reason in mathematics and prove things rigorously, couldn't really be answered inside a traditional academic setup. It needs a lot of compute, a strong engineering team, and people from very different backgrounds working closely together. At some point I understood that starting a company wasn't abandoning math. It was the most direct way to pursue the mathematical problem I cared about most. Once I saw it that way, the reluctance turned into a sense of obligation: if I believed this was possible and important, I should be the one to try.

r002.rationale: It says leaving her PhD path felt difficult, but does not characterize dropping out to start a company as impetuous.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, because I never saw myself as one. I grew up wanting to be a mathematician. My whole identity was built around proving things, around sitting with a hard problem for months and feeling that quiet satisfaction when it finally gives way. Entrepreneurship looked like the opposite of that to me. It seemed loud, it seemed fast, and it seemed like a world where you spend most of your time persuading people instead of thinking.

I also had a very concrete alternative path in front of me. I was doing a PhD at Stanford, I loved my advisors, and the academic track was something I understood. Leaving that felt like walking away from a very long investment, not just in years but in a kind of self-image. I think a lot of people from math or theory backgrounds share that hesitation. You worry that if you go build a company you will become a worse thinker, that you will lose the depth.

And there was a more personal fear too. When you are a researcher and your idea is wrong, you just write a different paper. When you are a founder and your idea is wrong, people who trusted you with their careers get hurt. That weight scared me more than failure itself.

What changed my mind was not that I suddenly fell in love with being a founder. It was that the thing I cared about, getting machines to really do mathematics, could not be done inside a paper anymore. It needed data, it needed engineering, it needed a team working on one problem for years. At some point I realized the question was not "do I want to be an entrepreneur" but "do I want this to exist." And once I framed it that way, the reluctance did not disappear, but it stopped mattering.

I wanted to feel prepared—to know that I had the right idea and that I could actually build something useful. But there’s no point at which you have all those answers. You have to be willing to start while you’re still figuring things out.

sol-6.1.text: I think I was reluctant because I loved working on ideas, and being an entrepreneur meant taking on a much broader responsibility. It wasn’t just, “Is this an interesting problem?” It was, “Can we build something people actually need, and can I bring a team together to do it?” I wasn’t sure I wanted that role. What eventually changed my mind was feeling that the problem mattered enough that I wanted to take responsibility for pursuing it.
